why.headline: A steady middle keeps you in one piece when you dive.

claims.text: When you dive, your trunk links your legs to your hands. A study of academy keepers looked at dives to each side. Dives to the weaker side showed less trunk control.
In the ready stance you hold still, then push off fast. Coaches of young players train the middle to steady spine and hips.
In studies with adults, a stiffer middle helped. It passed more hip power to arms and legs.
Keepers make only a few saves a match. Many are short, explosive dives and jumps. A middle that does not fold helps you land in control.
In a trial, pupils in their early teens trained twice a week. After 6 weeks, trunk strength tests were 8 to 22% better. Sideways jumping was 4 to 5% better.
Older elite youth players trained the trunk 2 to 3 times weekly. After 9 weeks, back strength was about 5% better. Short sprints were about 3% faster.

keep_up.text: Training about twice a week, as in your plan, keeps gains coming. In one youth study, jump gains lasted 8 weeks after training stopped. Everyone improves at their own pace.

map.plain: The long muscle down the front of your tummy
The muscles on the sides of your tummy

note.text: Plank studies measured these muscles in adults; none measured them in teens.

claims.text: The plank is a hold: your trunk stops your hips from sagging. In studies with adults, tummy muscles worked at under half effort.
Studies in young people find strength rises far more than muscle size. Early gains are mostly your nerves learning to switch muscles on.

limits.text: No study has tested the plank alone in goalkeepers. None shows it makes saves better. The teen trials used several trunk exercises and no untrained group.
Planks are part of the FIFA 11+ warm-up. A season-long youth trial linked the whole warm-up to fewer injuries. No trial shows the plank prevents injury on its own.
